intro: A puddle on the sidewalk is gone by afternoon. A nail left in the yard turns orange and crumbles. A candle burns down to nothing. A pouch of gray powder gets warm in your pocket. In each case something ordinary seems to vanish or change into something else, and in each case the same tiny pieces are still there, just rearranged or moving in a new way.

This unit is about those pieces. Everything you can touch is made of atoms far too small to see, joined into molecules or vast repeating patterns, always jiggling, sliding or flying depending on how much energy they have. You will follow the evidence that convinced scientists these pieces are real, from a botanist's dancing pollen to a physicist's formula, and you will use the site's microscope to see how far light can take you and where it stops.

Then you will watch atoms trade partners. Burning, rusting and fizzing are chemical reactions, and behind every one is a strict rule: atoms are never created or destroyed, only rearranged, and energy is either released or absorbed. By the end you will be able to explain why the Chicago fire of 1871 spread the way it did, why a hand warmer heats and a cold pack chills, and how to design and test a pouch of your own, safely.
bigQuestion: How can invisible particles and the way they rearrange explain everything from a melting ice cube to a city on fire?

timeline.t: Democritus proposes that matter is made of tiny uncuttable pieces moving in empty space.
Robert Boyle argues that an element should be defined by experiment, not by ancient lists of earth, air, fire and water.
Joseph Priestley isolates the gas later named oxygen and finds that a candle burns brilliantly in it.
Antoine Lavoisier publishes careful weighing experiments showing that mass is conserved in reactions.
John Dalton proposes that each element has its own kind of atom and that atoms combine in fixed ratios.
Robert Brown watches specks from pollen jitter endlessly in water and cannot explain it.
Michael Faraday gives his Christmas lectures on the chemical history of a candle.
Dmitri Mendeleev arranges the elements into a periodic table and predicts ones not yet found.
The Great Chicago Fire burns about three square miles; the city rebuilds in brick and stone.
Albert Einstein explains Brownian motion as the effect of unseen molecules striking a speck.
Jean Perrin measures the dance of tiny spheres and confirms Einstein's prediction; atoms are real.
The scanning tunneling microscope is invented and soon maps individual atoms as bumps on a surface.

test.q: Which statement about atoms is true?
choices: All matter is made of atoms, which are about 0.1 nanometer wide
Atoms can be seen with the site's light microscope
Only solids are made of atoms
Atoms were first observed by Robert Brown
test.why: Atoms are far smaller than light can show. Brown saw their effect on pollen specks, not the atoms themselves.

test.q: What does the formula CO2 describe?
choices: A mixture of carbon and oxygen
One molecule with one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms
Two carbon atoms and one oxygen atom
test.why: C with no number means one carbon; O2 means two oxygen atoms bonded to it in one molecule.

test.q: Which of these is a mixture?
test.why: Tap water contains dissolved minerals and gases along with water. The others are single substances.

test.q: In a gas, how are the particles arranged and moving?
choices: Far apart and flying freely in all directions
test.why: Gas particles are mostly empty space apart and move fast in every direction, which is why gases spread out.

test.q: A swimming pool at 25 °C and a cup of tea at 80 °C: which has more thermal energy?
choices: The pool, because it has vastly more particles
The tea, because it is hotter
test.why: Thermal energy is the total for all particles. The pool's enormous number of molecules outweighs the tea's higher temperature.

test.q: Why does the temperature of boiling water stop rising even on a high burner?
choices: The added energy goes into pulling molecules apart into gas instead of speeding them up
The pot absorbs the extra heat
test.why: During a change of state, energy is spent changing how particles are held, so the temperature holds steady.

test.q: Ice floats on Lake Michigan because
choices: ice is warmer than the water
frozen water molecules form an open pattern that makes ice less dense than liquid water
test.why: Ice has a density of about 0.92 g/cm³, less than water's 1.0, because of the spacing in its crystal pattern.

test.q: Why did Mendeleev's periodic table convince other chemists?
choices: It listed every element that would ever exist
It was the first chart of any kind
It was approved by the government
It predicted undiscovered elements, and they were later found as described
test.why: Gallium and germanium filled his gaps and matched his predictions, showing the pattern was real.

test.q: What finally convinced most scientists that molecules are real objects?
choices: Perrin's measurements of Brownian motion matched Einstein's prediction
Chemists agreed to believe in them
A light microscope photographed a molecule
test.why: A prediction that came out right, plus agreement between different ways of counting molecules, settled the question.

test.q: Which of these is a physical change?
test.why: Evaporation changes the state but not the substance. The other three make new substances.

test.q: In a chemical reaction, what happens to the atoms?
choices: Some are destroyed to make energy
They rearrange into new substances, and every atom is still there
test.why: Reactions only change which atoms are bonded to which. That is why mass is conserved.

test.q: A candle loses mass as it burns. Does this break the law of conservation of mass?
choices: No, because the flame turns mass into light
No, the products left as gases that were not weighed
test.why: Carbon dioxide and water vapor float away. Weigh them too and the total matches the wax plus the oxygen used.

test.q: What must a fire have to keep burning?
test.why: These three sides make up the fire triangle. Remove any one and combustion stops.

test.q: Baking soda and vinegar fizz, and the mixture gets cooler. What kind of process is this?
test.why: The mixture absorbs thermal energy from its surroundings, cooling them, so it is endothermic.

test.q: A hand warmer team wants a pouch that stays warm longer. What is the best next step?
choices: Switch to a fast, hot reaction
Add more of everything and skip measuring
Change one variable, such as pouch material, and measure the temperature over time
test.why: Testing one change at a time with a thermometer and a clock shows what actually helps.

Address the other side: what would someone who thinks the wax disappears point to, and how would you answer them?

title: Matter and Its Interactions

chapters.title: Atoms, Molecules and States of Matter
chapters.bigQuestion: If everything is made of particles too small to see, how do we know they are there and what they are doing?

story.title: The Pollen That Would Not Sit Still
story.kicker: In 1827 a careful botanist looked at pollen in water and saw something that no one could explain for almost eighty years.
paragraphs: Robert Brown was a Scottish botanist who spent his days sorting and naming plants. In the summer of 1827 he was studying pollen from a wildflower. He put a few grains in a drop of water, slid it under his microscope and leaned in. The grains were not sitting still. Tiny pieces that had broken off the pollen were jittering, jumping in short zigzag steps with no pattern at all.

Brown's first thought was the obvious one. Pollen comes from a living plant, so maybe the pieces were alive and swimming. He tested that idea. He tried pollen that had been stored dry for years. It jittered. He tried dust ground from rock, glass and even a chip of the Sphinx that a friend had brought from Egypt. Every tiny speck, alive or not, danced in the same restless way.

That killed the swimming idea. Something in the water itself had to be shoving the specks around. But the water looked perfectly still and perfectly clear. Brown published what he saw in 1828 and admitted that he could not explain it. For decades the jitter was just a curiosity that people called Brownian motion.

The answer came in 1905 from a young physicist named Albert Einstein. He worked out the math for what would happen if water were made of molecules far too small to see, all moving at random and knocking into anything floating among them. A speck of dust would get hit from every side, but never exactly evenly, so it would stagger around in just the zigzag Brown had drawn. Einstein predicted how far the specks should wander in a given time.

A few years later, the French physicist Jean Perrin measured the dance of tiny specks under his microscope and found that Einstein's numbers fit. It was the first solid measurement that showed atoms and molecules were real objects with real sizes, not just a handy idea. Brown had been watching the footprints of molecules all along.
story.think: Brown could not see water molecules, yet he was seeing what they did. What is another case where you can know something is there only by its effects?

lessons.title: Everything Is Made of Atoms
lessons.mainIdea: All matter is built from atoms, which are far too small to see but real enough to measure.
reading: Take a lump of aluminum foil and tear it in half. Tear a piece in half again, and again. You can keep going for a long time, but not forever. Eventually you would reach a single *atom* of aluminum, and if you split that, you would no longer have aluminum at all. An atom is the smallest piece of a substance that is still that substance. Every solid, liquid and gas around you is built from atoms.

Atoms are astonishingly small. A typical atom is about one tenth of a nanometer across, and a nanometer is one billionth of a meter. A human hair is roughly a million atoms wide. There are more atoms in one drop of water than there are drops of water in Lake Michigan. No light microscope can show a single atom, which is why the idea of atoms was argued about for more than two thousand years.

An *element* is a substance made of only one kind of atom. Gold is an element: every atom in a gold ring is a gold atom. Oxygen, iron, carbon and hydrogen are elements too. About ninety elements occur naturally on Earth, and scientists have made a few dozen more in laboratories. All the millions of different materials you know are combinations of these few kinds of atoms.

The word atom comes from a Greek word meaning uncuttable. Around 400 BCE the Greek thinker Democritus suggested that matter was made of tiny uncuttable pieces. They moved, he said, through empty space. He had no way to test it. Real evidence had to wait for careful weighing in chemistry. Finally it came from Brown's dancing specks and the measurements that explained them.

words.d: the smallest piece of an element that still has that element's properties
a substance made of only one kind of atom, such as gold or oxygen
one billionth of a meter; a typical atom is about one tenth of a nanometer wide

look.title: An Ancient Guess
look.text: Democritus argued that things like sweet, bitter, hot, cold and color exist only by agreement among people. In truth, he said, there are only atoms and the empty space they move through.
look.cite: Democritus, as reported by later Greek writers, about 400 BCE (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Democritus had no microscope and no experiments. Why might people have doubted his idea for so long, even if it turned out to be close to right?

check.q: What is an element?
choices: A substance made of only one kind of atom
A mixture of two kinds of atoms
The smallest piece of any substance
check.why: An element contains just one kind of atom. Gold is all gold atoms; oxygen is all oxygen atoms.

check.q: About how wide is a human hair, measured in atoms?
check.why: A hair is roughly 0.1 millimeter wide and an atom is about 0.1 nanometer, so about a million atoms fit across it.

check.q: Why was the idea of atoms argued about for over two thousand years?
choices: Atoms did not exist until recently
No one could see atoms, so there was no direct evidence
check.why: Atoms are too small to see with any light microscope. Convincing evidence came only from careful measurements much later.

lessons.title: Molecules and Extended Structures
lessons.mainIdea: Atoms bond together either in small fixed groups called molecules or in huge repeating patterns called extended structures.
reading: Water is not an element. Every drop is made of tiny groups, each with two hydrogen atoms attached to one oxygen atom. A group of atoms joined together this way is called a *molecule*. Water molecules are all identical, and the formula H2O is a short way to say what is in each one. Oxygen in the air also comes in molecules, pairs of oxygen atoms written O2. Carbon dioxide is one carbon atom joined to two oxygen atoms, CO2.

Molecules can be tiny or huge. A hydrogen molecule has just two atoms. The sugar in candy, called sucrose, has 45 atoms per molecule. The proteins in your muscles have thousands of atoms each, all linked in a specific order. In every case the molecule is a unit: the atoms inside it are held together by *bonds*, which are strong attractions between atoms, and the molecule moves around as one piece.

Some substances are not made of separate molecules at all. Table salt is sodium and chlorine atoms arranged in a repeating grid that goes on and on in every direction, like a stack of tiny cubes. There is no single salt molecule, only the pattern. Chemists call this an *extended structure*. A diamond is one giant extended structure of carbon atoms, each bonded to four neighbors, which is why diamond is so hard. A metal like iron is also an extended structure, with atoms packed in orderly layers.

Under the microscope you cannot see the atoms, but you can see the results. Salt grains are little cubes because the atoms inside are arranged in cubes. Snowflakes have six arms because water molecules lock into a six-sided pattern when they freeze. The shape you can see is a clue to the pattern you cannot.

words.d: a group of two or more atoms bonded together that moves as one unit
a strong attraction that holds atoms together
a substance whose atoms form a repeating pattern that goes on and on, with no separate molecules

look.title: Salt Under the Lens
look.text: Put a few grains of table salt under the site's microscope at low power. Most grains are little boxes with flat faces and square corners, even the broken ones. Now look at sugar grains. They are also crystals, but their faces meet at slanted angles rather than square corners.
look.prompt: Salt and sugar are both made of atoms bonded in patterns. What does the difference in the crystal shapes tell you about the two patterns?

check.q: What does the formula H2O tell you about a water molecule?
choices: It is made of two kinds of molecules
It has two oxygen atoms and one hydrogen atom
It has twenty atoms in total
It has two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom
check.why: The 2 after H means two hydrogen atoms; the O with no number means one oxygen atom.

check.q: Why is table salt described as an extended structure rather than a molecule?
choices: Its atoms form a repeating grid with no separate units
It has more than ten atoms
check.why: In salt, sodium and chlorine atoms repeat in a pattern that goes on in every direction. There is no single salt molecule.

check.q: Salt grains look like tiny cubes. What is the best explanation?
choices: Salt is cut into cubes at the factory
The atoms inside are arranged in a cube-shaped pattern
Cubes are the easiest shape for any crystal
Water shapes the salt as it dries
check.why: The visible shape of a crystal reflects the invisible arrangement of its atoms. Salt's atoms sit in a cubic grid.

lessons.title: Pure Substances and Mixtures
lessons.mainIdea: A pure substance has one kind of particle throughout, while a mixture holds several kinds that can be separated without a chemical change.
reading: Pour a glass of tap water and a glass of distilled water. They look the same, but they are not. Distilled water is a *pure substance*: every particle in it is a water molecule. Tap water is a *mixture*. It has water molecules plus dissolved minerals, a little chlorine added to kill germs, and some dissolved air. A pure substance is either a single element, like copper, or a single compound, like water or salt.

A *compound* is a pure substance made of two or more elements joined in a fixed ratio. Water is always two hydrogen to one oxygen. Salt is always one sodium to one chlorine. Because the ratio never changes, a compound has its own fixed properties. Pure water always freezes at 0 °C and boils at about 100 °C at sea level. Change the ratio and you have a different compound with different properties: hydrogen peroxide, H2O2, is not water and will bleach your hair.

Mixtures are different. Salt water can be a little salty or very salty. You can pull the salt back out by letting the water evaporate. Air is a mixture of nitrogen, oxygen, argon, carbon dioxide and water vapor. The amounts shift from place to place. The parts of a mixture keep their own properties. So you can separate them by physical means: filtering, evaporating, using a magnet, or letting the heavier bits settle.

Scientists use *models* to picture these ideas. A model is a simplified picture of something you cannot see directly. Draw water as pairs of circles stuck together, all the same. Draw salt water as those pairs with a few different circles scattered among them. The drawing is not the real thing, but it captures the key difference: one kind of particle or several.

words.d: matter made of only one kind of particle, either an element or a compound
a pure substance made of two or more elements joined in a fixed ratio
matter that holds two or more substances that keep their own properties and can be separated
a simplified picture or description of something that helps explain how it works

look.title: The Kitchen Test
look.text: On the counter are four things: a cup of sugar, a cup of sweet tea, a copper penny made before 1982, and a handful of gravel from the driveway. You can look, stir, filter, and heat gently. You cannot use any chemical reactions.
look.prompt: Sort the four into pure substances and mixtures. For each mixture, describe one physical way you could separate its parts.

check.q: Which of these is a pure substance?
check.why: Distilled water is only water molecules. Air, tap water and sweet tea each contain several substances mixed together.

check.q: What makes a compound different from a mixture?
choices: A compound is always a liquid
A compound contains only one element
A compound can be separated by filtering
A compound's elements are joined in a fixed ratio
check.why: Water is always two hydrogen to one oxygen. A mixture like salt water can hold any amount of salt.

check.q: Salt water is left in a pan until the water evaporates and salt is left behind. What does this show?
choices: Salt water is a mixture that can be separated physically
Salt and water are the same substance
check.why: The salt kept its own properties and came back out with no chemical change, which is the mark of a mixture.

lessons.title: Solids, Liquids and Gases
lessons.mainIdea: The three common states of matter differ in how tightly particles are held and how freely they move.
reading: An ice cube, a glass of water and the steam over a pot are all the same substance, H2O. What changes is not the molecules but how they move. In a *solid* the particles are packed close together and locked in place. They still jiggle, but each one only vibrates around a fixed spot. That is why a solid keeps its shape and its volume. You cannot pour ice.

In a *liquid* the particles are still close together, almost touching, but they are no longer locked. They slide past one another and tumble around. A liquid keeps its volume but takes the shape of whatever holds it, so water fills a glass to the bottom and flows down a drain. Because the particles stay close, you cannot squeeze a liquid into a much smaller space.

In a *gas* the particles are far apart and fly freely. They bounce off the walls and off each other. Most of a gas is empty space. A gas spreads out to fill any container and has no shape of its own. It can easily be squeezed smaller, which is why you can pump more air into a bike tire. At room temperature the molecules in air move at roughly 500 meters per second. That is faster than the speed of sound.

The state of a substance depends on a tug-of-war. The particles attract one another and want to stick. Their motion tries to shake them apart. When motion is weak, attraction wins and you get a solid. When motion is stronger, the particles break free but stay near: a liquid. When motion wins completely, the particles fly off: a gas.

words.d: a state of matter in which particles are packed close and vibrate in fixed positions
a state of matter in which particles stay close but slide past one another
a state of matter in which particles are far apart and move freely in all directions

look.title: A Room Full of Students
look.text: Picture a gym class. First everyone stands in tight rows, marching in place. Then the teacher says free time, and students wander around the gym in groups, bumping shoulders but staying together. Finally the doors open, and they scatter across the whole playground at a run.
look.prompt: Match each part of the scene to a solid, a liquid and a gas. What does the teacher's instruction stand for in the real world?

check.q: Why does a solid keep its shape?
choices: Its particles are not moving at all
Its particles vibrate in fixed positions and cannot slide past each other
check.why: Solid particles jiggle but stay locked in place, so the whole object keeps its shape.

check.q: Why can you pump extra air into a bike tire but not extra water into a full bottle?
choices: Gas particles are far apart with empty space between them, while liquid particles are already close together
Air is not made of particles
check.why: A gas is mostly empty space, so it can be compressed. Liquid particles already nearly touch.

check.q: What decides whether a substance is a solid, a liquid or a gas?
choices: The balance between how strongly its particles attract and how fast they move
check.why: When attraction wins, the particles lock into a solid; when motion wins, they fly apart as a gas.

lessons.title: Temperature and Thermal Energy
lessons.mainIdea: Temperature measures how fast particles are moving on average, while thermal energy is the total motion energy of all the particles in an object.
reading: Hold a cup of hot cocoa. What is the difference between it and the same cocoa after it cools? The molecules are the same. What changed is how fast they move. *Temperature* is a measure of the average speed of the particles in a substance. Hot cocoa has fast-moving molecules; cold cocoa has slower ones. When you feel heat, you are feeling fast particles bumping into your skin.

Every particle in motion carries *kinetic energy*, the energy of movement. Add up the kinetic energy of every particle in an object and you get its *thermal energy*. Thermal energy depends on two things: how fast the particles move and how many there are. A bathtub of warm water has far more thermal energy than a cup of boiling water. The cup is hotter, but the tub holds so many more molecules.

Thermal energy moves from hotter things to colder things, never the other way on its own. Fast particles in the hot object collide with slow particles in the cold one. They pass on some of their motion. Drop an ice cube into lemonade. The fast lemonade molecules hit the slow ice molecules and speed them up. The lemonade molecules slow down. The lemonade cools and the ice warms until both reach the same temperature.

Temperature has a floor. If you could slow particles down until they had the least motion possible, you would reach about −273 °C, called absolute zero. Nothing can be colder, because you cannot take away motion that is not there. There is no ceiling. Inside the sun, particles move so fast that the temperature is millions of degrees.

words.d: a measure of the average kinetic energy, or speed, of the particles in a substance
the energy an object or particle has because it is moving
the total kinetic energy of all the particles in an object

look.title: The Cup and the Lake
look.text: A cup of coffee is at 80 °C. Lake Michigan in August is about 20 °C. Pour the coffee into the lake and the lake's temperature does not change in any way you could measure. But if you poured the lake into the coffee, the coffee would instantly be lake temperature.
look.prompt: Which has the higher temperature, and which has more thermal energy? Explain why the two answers are different.

check.q: What does temperature measure?
choices: The average speed of the particles in a substance
How much space an object takes up
check.why: Temperature tells you the average kinetic energy of the particles. Faster particles mean a higher temperature.

check.q: A cup of boiling water and a warm bathtub: which has more thermal energy, and why?
choices: The cup, because it is hotter
The bathtub, because it has many more particles even though each moves more slowly
They are equal because both contain water
The cup, because it has fewer particles
check.why: Thermal energy is the total for all particles. The tub's huge number of molecules outweighs the cup's higher temperature.

check.q: An ice cube is dropped into warm juice. What happens to the energy?
choices: Cold flows from the ice into the juice
The ice gains energy from the air only
Energy passes from the fast juice molecules to the slow ice molecules until they match
Nothing moves until the ice melts
check.why: Thermal energy always moves from hotter to colder. Collisions speed up the ice's particles and slow down the juice's.

lessons.title: Changes of State
lessons.mainIdea: Melting, boiling, freezing and condensing are the same particles gaining or losing enough energy to change how they move.
reading: Leave an ice cube on the counter and it melts. Leave the puddle and it disappears. Nothing was destroyed. The water molecules first gained enough energy to slide instead of vibrating, which is *melting*. Then, one at a time, the fastest molecules at the surface broke free into the air, which is *evaporation*. Heat water on a stove and bubbles of vapor form throughout the liquid: that is boiling, evaporation happening everywhere at once.

Every change of state is a change in particle motion. Add energy and particles move faster: solid to liquid to gas. Take energy away and they slow down: gas to liquid to solid. When water vapor in warm breath hits a cold window, the molecules slow, stick together and form droplets. That is *condensation*. When a puddle cools below 0 °C on a January night in Chicago, the molecules lock into a pattern. That is freezing.

Some solids skip the liquid step. Dry ice, which is frozen carbon dioxide, turns straight into gas at about −78 °C, a change called *sublimation*. That is why it makes fog without leaving a puddle. Frost on a windowpane forms the opposite way: water vapor turns directly to ice crystals without ever being liquid. Even ordinary ice cubes slowly shrink in a freezer as molecules sublime off the surface.

Each pure substance changes state at its own temperatures. Water melts at 0 °C and boils at about 100 °C at sea level. Iron does not melt until 1538 °C. Oxygen is a gas at any temperature you will ever feel, because it boils at −183 °C. These fixed temperatures are so reliable that they are used to identify a substance and to check whether it is pure.

words.d: the change from solid to liquid as particles gain enough energy to slide past one another
the change from liquid to gas at the surface, as the fastest particles escape
the change from gas to liquid as particles slow down and cling together
the change from solid directly to gas without becoming a liquid

look.title: Melting Points of Some Substances
look.prompt: Which of these substances are solid on a −20 °C Chicago morning? Which ones are solid on a 30 °C summer afternoon? What does the difference between mercury and iron suggest about how strongly their atoms attract?

check.q: What happens to water molecules when ice melts?
choices: They break apart into hydrogen and oxygen
They gain enough energy to slide past each other instead of vibrating in place
check.why: Melting is a change in motion, not in the molecules themselves. The same H2O molecules become free to slide.

check.q: Water droplets form on the outside of a cold glass on a humid day. Where does the water come from?
choices: Water vapor in the air that slowed down and condensed on the cold surface
The ice inside the glass melting through
check.why: The cold glass slows the water vapor molecules in the air until they cling together as liquid drops.

check.q: Dry ice fogs but never leaves a puddle. Why?
choices: It sublimes, going straight from solid to gas
The fog is smoke, not gas
check.why: Frozen carbon dioxide changes directly to gas at about −78 °C, skipping the liquid state.

lessons.title: Energy In, Energy Out
lessons.mainIdea: While a substance is changing state, added energy goes into breaking particles loose, so the temperature holds steady until the change is done.
reading: Put a pot of ice on the stove with a thermometer in it. At first the temperature climbs steadily. Then, at 0 °C, something odd happens: the thermometer stops rising while the ice melts, even though the burner is still on. Only when the last ice is gone does the temperature start to climb again. It rises to about 100 °C, and then it stalls again while the water boils, no matter how high you turn the heat.

The stall happens because the energy has a different job. Before the ice melts, added energy makes the molecules vibrate faster, which raises the temperature. At 0 °C, the added energy goes into breaking the molecules loose from their fixed positions instead of speeding them up. It takes a lot of energy to free every molecule, and the temperature cannot rise until that is finished. The same thing happens at the boiling point, where energy is spent pulling molecules fully apart from one another.

This is why sweating cools you. Each water molecule that evaporates from your skin has to take a chunk of energy with it, and it takes that energy from you. It is also why a pot of boiling water is not hotter on a bigger burner. It just boils faster. And it is why steam burns worse than boiling water: steam at 100 °C carries all the extra energy it took to boil, and it gives that energy back when it condenses on your skin.

Scientists draw this as a *heating curve*. It is a graph of temperature against time, with flat steps at each change of state. The steps are the fingerprints of a substance. The height of each step is the melting or boiling point. The length of each flat part shows how much energy the change costs.

words.d: a graph of temperature over time as a substance is heated, with flat steps at each change of state
the temperature at which a liquid changes to gas throughout, not just at the surface

look.title: The Thermometer That Stopped
look.text: Maria heats a beaker of crushed ice and records the temperature every minute. Minutes 0 to 4: −10, −6, −2, 0, 0. Minutes 5 to 9: 0, 0, 0, 3, 8. Minutes 10 to 14: 20, 35, 50, 65, 80. Minutes 15 to 19: 95, 100, 100, 100, 100.
look.prompt: Where on this list is the ice melting? Where is the water boiling? What was the added energy doing during the flat parts?

check.q: A pot of ice water sits on a hot burner, but the thermometer stays at 0 °C for several minutes. Why?
choices: The added energy is freeing molecules from the solid instead of speeding them up
check.why: During melting, energy goes into breaking molecules loose from their fixed places, so temperature does not rise until all the ice is gone.

check.q: Why does sweating cool your skin?
choices: Sweat is colder than your body
Each evaporating molecule takes energy from your skin as it leaves
check.why: Evaporation costs energy. The escaping water molecules take it from your skin, which cools you.

check.q: On a heating curve, what does a flat part of the line show?
choices: A change of state is happening
The burner has been turned off
check.why: The line goes flat while energy is being used to change state, since the temperature holds steady during melting or boiling.

lessons.title: Density: How Tightly Packed
lessons.mainIdea: Density is mass divided by volume, and it explains why some things float and others sink.
reading: Drop a steel bolt and a cork into a bucket. The bolt sinks, the cork floats. It is not about weight alone: a huge log floats, while a tiny pebble sinks. What matters is how much *mass* is packed into each bit of space. That quantity is *density*. To find it, divide the mass of an object by its *volume*, the amount of space it fills. Water has a density of about 1 gram per cubic centimeter, so a sugar-cube-sized piece of water has a mass of about 1 gram.

Anything less dense than water floats in it. Anything more dense sinks. Cork is about 0.24 g/cm³, so it floats high. Iron is about 7.9 g/cm³, so it sinks fast. Gold is about 19.3 g/cm³, nearly twenty times denser than water, which is why a gold bar the size of a brick is surprisingly hard to lift. A steel ship floats because it is mostly hollow, full of air, so its mass divided by its whole volume is less than water's.

Density is a property of the substance, not of the amount. A drop of mercury and a jar of mercury have the same density. That makes density useful for identifying a material. Archimedes, an ancient Greek, is said to have used this idea to test whether a king's crown was pure gold, by comparing its mass to the water it pushed aside.

Density depends on the particles and how they are packed. Gold atoms are heavy and packed tightly. Cork is full of tiny air pockets. Ice is less dense than liquid water, about 0.92 g/cm³, because water molecules lock into an open six-sided pattern when they freeze, leaving more space between them. That is why ice floats on Lake Michigan instead of sinking to the bottom, and why the fish survive under it.

words.d: the mass of a substance divided by its volume; how much matter is packed into each unit of space
the amount of matter in an object, measured in grams or kilograms
the amount of space an object takes up, measured in cubic centimeters or liters

look.title: Density of Some Common Materials
look.prompt: Which of these would float in water? An aluminum can and an iron nail both sink, but which sinks faster in thick syrup? What would you expect if you could weigh a gold coin and an aluminum coin of the same size?

check.q: How do you calculate density?
check.why: Density is mass per unit of volume, so you divide the mass by the volume.

check.q: Why does ice float on water?
choices: Frozen water molecules lock into an open pattern, so ice is less dense than liquid water
Ice is lighter because some molecules escape
check.why: Water molecules form a six-sided pattern with extra space when they freeze, making ice about 0.92 g/cm³.

check.q: A large log floats but a small pebble sinks. What does this show?
choices: The pebble has more mass than the log
Floating depends on density, not on total mass
check.why: The log has more total mass but less mass per unit of volume than water. The dense pebble sinks.

lessons.title: The Periodic Table
lessons.mainIdea: The periodic table arranges every element by the number of protons in its atoms, and elements in the same column behave in similar ways.
reading: Every science classroom has the same chart on the wall: rows and columns of boxes, each with a symbol and a number. That is the *periodic table*, a map of all the known elements. Each box is one element. H is hydrogen, O is oxygen, Fe is iron, Au is gold. The symbols come from the element's name, sometimes its Latin name, which is why iron is Fe from ferrum.

The number in each box is the element's *atomic number*. It is the count of protons in the center of one of its atoms. Hydrogen has 1 proton, helium 2, carbon 6, oxygen 8, iron 26, gold 79. That number is what makes an element what it is. Every atom with 6 protons is carbon, no matter what. The table simply lists the elements in order from 1 up to 118.

The table is not just a list. It is folded into rows so that elements with similar behavior land in the same column. The far left column holds soft metals like sodium and potassium that react violently with water. The far right holds gases like helium, neon and argon that almost never react at all. Fluorine, chlorine and bromine sit in one column and all form similar compounds with sodium.

The Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev built the first version of this chart in 1869. He arranged the 63 elements known then in order and lined up the ones that acted alike. He left gaps where the pattern told him an element was missing. He even predicted what those missing elements would be like. Gallium and germanium were found in the following years. They matched his predictions closely. The table had turned from a filing system into a tool that could predict.

words.d: a chart of all the elements arranged by atomic number, with similar elements in the same column
the number of protons in an atom, which identifies the element
a positively charged particle in the center of an atom

look.title: Mendeleev Predicts
look.text: In his 1869 paper Mendeleev wrote that if the elements are arranged by their atomic weights, their properties repeat in a regular, periodic pattern. He added that the pattern let him expect the discovery of several new elements whose properties he could describe in advance.
look.cite: Dmitri Mendeleev, on the periodic law, 1869 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Mendeleev's chart made predictions that later turned out true. Why does a successful prediction count as stronger evidence than a chart that only describes what is already known?

check.q: What does an element's atomic number tell you?
choices: The number of protons in one of its atoms
How many elements it can bond with
check.why: The atomic number is the proton count. Every atom with 8 protons is oxygen.

check.q: Why are sodium and potassium in the same column of the periodic table?
choices: They were discovered in the same year
They behave in similar ways, both reacting strongly with water
They have the same atomic number
check.why: The table is folded so that elements with similar behavior line up in columns.

check.q: What was most convincing about Mendeleev's table?
choices: It was the first list of elements
It predicted undiscovered elements, and they were later found as described
check.why: Gallium and germanium filled the gaps he left and matched his predictions, showing the pattern was real.

lessons.title: The Limits of the Microscope
lessons.mainIdea: A light microscope cannot show anything much smaller than the wavelength of light, so atoms need other tools.
reading: The site's microscope can show you a cell, the hairs on a fly's leg, the cubes of a salt grain. Turn up the magnification and eventually the image goes soft and blurry no matter how good the lens is. That is not a flaw in the instrument. It is a limit of light itself. Light travels as waves, and a visible light wave is a few hundred *nanometers* long. Anything much smaller than that cannot be picked out clearly, the way ocean waves roll right past a pebble without showing where it is.

The finest detail a light microscope can separate is about 200 nanometers. A bacterium is around 1,000 nanometers, so it shows up. A typical virus is around 100 nanometers, so it is a blur at best. An atom is about 0.1 nanometer, two thousand times smaller than the limit. No lens made of glass will ever show one.

In the 1930s scientists built the *electron microscope*. It uses a beam of electrons instead of light. Electrons can act as waves with wavelengths thousands of times shorter than light. So the limit drops far enough to see viruses and, in the best instruments, rows of atoms. In 1981 a different tool arrived, the scanning tunneling microscope. It traced the surface of a metal with a needle so sharp its tip was a single atom. It mapped individual atoms as bumps.

Brown's microscope in 1827 could not see molecules and never will. What it could see was their effect: the shove of unseen molecules on a visible speck. Much of science works this way. You cannot see the wind, but you can watch the trees. Knowing the limit of your instrument is part of using it well.

words.d: one billionth of a meter; visible light waves are a few hundred nanometers long
a microscope that uses a beam of electrons instead of light to see far smaller details

look.title: How Small Is Small?
look.prompt: Which items on the list could the site's light microscope show clearly? About how many atoms would fit across one bacterium?

check.q: Why can't a light microscope show an atom, no matter how good the lens is?
choices: Atoms move too fast to photograph
Atoms are far smaller than the wavelength of light, so light waves cannot pick them out
check.why: Light waves are a few hundred nanometers long; an atom is about 0.1 nanometer. The limit is in the light, not the lens.

check.q: Which of these could a light microscope show clearly?
check.why: The light microscope limit is about 200 nanometers. Only the bacterium is bigger than that.

check.q: How does an electron microscope see smaller things than a light microscope?
choices: It uses a much bigger lens
It uses electrons, whose waves are far shorter than light waves
check.why: Shorter waves can pick out smaller details. Electron waves can be thousands of times shorter than light waves.

lessons.title: Evidence That Atoms Are Real
lessons.mainIdea: Brownian motion, explained by Einstein and measured by Perrin, showed that molecules are real objects whose size can be calculated.
reading: For most of the 1800s, chemists used atoms the way an accountant uses columns: a handy way to keep the books. John Dalton had shown in 1808 that elements combine in fixed whole-number ratios. That is exactly what you would expect if atoms were real and each kind had its own mass. But some respected scientists still insisted that atoms were only a useful story. No one had ever seen one. Perhaps the ratios could be explained some other way.

*Brownian motion*, the jitter Robert Brown saw in 1827, turned out to be the key. In 1905 Albert Einstein reasoned about what would happen if water were made of molecules in constant random motion. A visible speck would be hit unevenly from moment to moment. It would wander in a zigzag. He did not just say so. He derived a formula. The distance a speck should drift depends on the temperature, the size of the speck, the thickness of the liquid, and the number of molecules in a gram of water.

Between 1908 and 1913, Jean Perrin put the formula to the test. He made tiny spheres of gum resin, all nearly the same size, watched them through a microscope and marked their positions every thirty seconds on graph paper. The wandering matched Einstein's prediction. Better still, Perrin could work backward from the wandering to count how many molecules are in a gram of water. Several completely different methods gave nearly the same count. That agreement convinced almost everyone.

This is how a good *theory* earns its place. It explains an old puzzle, it predicts a number no one has measured yet, and the measurement comes out right. Perrin received the Nobel Prize in 1926 for proving, as the citation put it, the discontinuous structure of matter. The dancing specks that puzzled a botanist had become the proof that the world is made of pieces.

words.d: the random jittering of tiny specks in a liquid or gas, caused by molecules hitting them unevenly
a well-tested explanation that fits the evidence and makes predictions that can be checked
a statement about what a measurement should show if an explanation is right

look.title: Brown Reports What He Saw
look.text: Brown wrote that while examining pollen grains suspended in water, he saw many of the small particles clearly in motion. Their movement, he reported, came neither from currents in the fluid nor from its slow evaporation, but belonged to the particles themselves.
look.cite: Robert Brown, A Brief Account of Microscopical Observations, 1828 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Brown ruled out currents and evaporation before he published. Why is it important to rule out ordinary explanations first, and what would Einstein later say the motion belonged to?

check.q: What did Einstein's 1905 paper add to Brown's observation?
choices: A formula predicting how far a speck should wander if water is made of moving molecules
A drawing of a water molecule
check.why: Einstein turned the idea into a testable number: the expected drift of a speck, based on invisible molecular collisions.

check.q: Why did Perrin's measurements convince scientists that atoms were real?
choices: The speck motion matched Einstein's prediction, and the molecule count agreed with other methods
check.why: When a prediction is confirmed and different methods give the same number, the explanation is very likely right.

check.q: Which best describes why a theory earns trust in science?
choices: It explains old puzzles and its predictions come out right when tested
It is written by a famous scientist
check.why: Trust comes from explaining evidence and surviving tests, not from who says it or how simple it is.

review.q: Which statement about atoms is correct?
choices: Atoms can be seen with a good light microscope
Every substance is made of atoms, which are far too small to see with light
Only metals are made of atoms
Atoms were first seen by Democritus
review.why: All matter is made of atoms. They are about 0.1 nanometer wide, far below what light can show.

review.q: Diamond is described as an extended structure. What does that mean?
choices: It is a single large molecule that moves as a unit
Its carbon atoms form a repeating pattern that continues throughout, with no separate molecules
It is made of many elements
review.why: In an extended structure the bonded pattern goes on and on. There is no individual diamond molecule.
Air holds nitrogen, oxygen, argon and other gases that keep their own properties. The others are pure substances.

review.q: In which state are particles close together but able to slide past one another?
review.why: Liquid particles stay close but are not locked in place, which is why liquids flow.

review.q: A thermometer in melting ice reads 0 °C for five minutes while a burner runs. What is the added energy doing?

Nothing, because ice cannot absorb energy
review.why: During a change of state, energy goes into changing how particles are held, not into raising the temperature.

review.q: A block has a mass of 27 grams and a volume of 10 cubic centimeters. What is its density and will it sink in water?

review.q: What do the elements in one column of the periodic table have in common?
